nodes.title: Service registration and discovery: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Consul keeps a live catalog of which service instances exist and where. Services register themselves (or are registered by an agent/orchestrator), health checks decide who is healthy, and other services discover them by name via DNS or HTTP.

flashcards.front: How does a service get into the Consul catalog?
flashcards.back: By registration with the local Consul agent — through a service definition file, the HTTP API, or an orchestrator integration. Each registration includes the service name, address/port, optional tags, and one or more health checks.

flashcards.front: Why are health checks essential to discovery?
flashcards.back: Discovery should only return instances that can actually serve traffic. Consul runs checks (HTTP, TCP, script, TTL) and removes failing instances from DNS/API results, so callers never get routed to a dead node — discovery and health are inseparable.

flashcards.front: How do clients discover a service?
flashcards.back: Two interfaces over the same catalog: DNS (e.g. web.service.consul resolves to healthy instances) for zero-code integration, or the HTTP API for richer queries and tag filtering. Prepared queries add failover and load-balancing policy.

flashcards.front: What does an agent vs a server do in Consul?
flashcards.back: Every node runs a Consul agent; client agents forward registrations and checks to the servers. Servers (a Raft quorum, typically 3 or 5) hold the authoritative catalog and KV state. Keeping an odd number of servers preserves quorum during failures.

questions.q: You are deploying a new Consul datacenter for production and want the control plane to tolerate the loss of one server while preserving Raft quorum. What is the minimum number of Consul server agents that HashiCorp recommends for this datacenter?
choices: 1 server agent
3 server agents
5 server agents
7 server agents
questions.explanation: Consul servers participate in a Raft cluster, which requires a strict majority (quorum) to commit writes and elect a leader. With 3 servers, quorum is 2, so the cluster tolerates the failure of any 1 server — the documented recommended minimum for production. A single server has no fault tolerance and is dev-only; 5 servers (quorum 3) is the recommended size when you need to survive 2 simultaneous failures; and 7 servers is generally the practical upper bound because adding members beyond that slows Raft replication without adding meaningful fault tolerance.

questions.q: Which protocol does the Consul server cluster use to elect a leader and keep the service catalog, KV store, and ACL state strongly consistent across the servers in a datacenter?
choices: Raft consensus
Serf gossip
Paxos consensus
BGP route reflection
questions.explanation: Consul servers use the Raft consensus protocol to elect a single leader and replicate a strongly consistent log of state changes for the catalog, KV store, sessions and ACLs. Serf gossip handles membership and failure detection between all agents but is eventually consistent, not strongly consistent. Paxos is a different consensus family that Consul does not use, and BGP is an Internet routing protocol unrelated to Consul replication.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the LAN gossip pool in a Consul datacenter?
choices: Replicate KV writes between server agents in the datacenter
Forward client DNS queries from agents to the upstream resolver
Provide membership awareness and failure detection across all Consul agents in the datacenter
Synchronize ACL tokens between the primary and secondary datacenters
questions.explanation: Consul's LAN gossip pool, built on Serf, lets every server and client agent in a datacenter learn which peers are alive, detect failures quickly and propagate basic membership events. KV replication and other strongly consistent state changes ride on Raft between servers, not on gossip; DNS queries are answered locally by the agent rather than gossiped; and cross-datacenter ACL token replication uses ACL replication over the WAN, not the LAN gossip pool.

questions.q: A platform team wants applications running as systemd units on bare-metal hosts to be registered with Consul without modifying application code. Which is the most idiomatic registration method?
choices: Embed a call to the Consul HTTP /v1/agent/service/register endpoint in the application's startup logic
Write the service identity into the Consul KV store and have the agent watch the key
Create a Kubernetes Service object referencing each application host
Place a service definition in a JSON or HCL file inside the agent's configuration directory so the local agent registers it on startup
questions.explanation: On non-orchestrated hosts, the standard pattern is to drop a service definition file (for example `web.json` or `web.hcl`) into the agent's configuration directory; the local Consul agent reads it at startup or on a reload and registers the service in the catalog. Calling the HTTP API from the application requires code changes and re-registration logic that the team explicitly wants to avoid; the KV store does not auto-register services; and Kubernetes Service objects apply only inside a Kubernetes cluster, not to systemd workloads on bare metal.

nodes.title: Command-line tooling: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Most exam workflows involve `aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, or `kubectl`. Knowing the structure of each (resource → command → flags) saves you in the lab portion and in real life. They're all roughly the same shape with different naming conventions.

flashcards.front: How do you authenticate the AWS CLI?
flashcards.back: `aws configure` writes credentials to `~/.aws/credentials` (access key + secret) and `~/.aws/config` (region, output format). Use named profiles for multi-account: `aws s3 ls --profile prod`. Prefer `aws configure sso` or temporary STS credentials over long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does `kubectl get` do, and what flags are essential?
flashcards.back: Lists resources of a kind: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get nodes`. Key flags: `-n <namespace>` (default is `default`), `-o wide` (more columns), `-o yaml` (full manifest), `--watch` (live updates), `-l label=value` (filter by label).

AWS / Azure / gcloud all support `--output json|text|table|yaml`. JSON is for piping into `jq` for scripts. Table is for humans browsing in the terminal. Always set a default in your config so you don't squint at JSON when browsing.

flashcards.front: How do you find a command's options without leaving the terminal?
flashcards.back: `aws <service> <command> help` (or `--help`), `kubectl <verb> --help`, `az <group> <command> --help`. These open built-in docs with every flag listed. Searching the official web docs is for concepts; for syntax, the local help is always current.

questions.q: A web service is registered with Consul and has an HTTP health check that calls `/health` every 10 seconds. The check starts returning a non-2xx response and Consul marks the instance critical. What is the effect on service discovery by default?
choices: Consul deletes the service definition from the catalog until the operator re-registers it
Consul stops returning that instance in healthy DNS and HTTP queries while the check remains critical, but other healthy instances of the same service are still returned
All other instances of the same service are also marked critical until the failing instance recovers
Consul automatically restarts the underlying application process on the host
questions.explanation: When a check is critical, Consul keeps the registration in the catalog but excludes that specific instance from the healthy results returned by DNS lookups and the `/v1/health/service/<name>?passing` API; consumers can still reach the other healthy instances. Consul does not delete service definitions on a failing check, it does not cascade the failure to peer instances, and it has no built-in capability to restart the underlying application — health checks only inform discovery and operators.

questions.q: Using the Consul CLI, which command stores the string `true` under the key `web/maintenance` in the KV store?
choices: consul write web/maintenance true
consul config write web/maintenance true
consul kv put web/maintenance true
consul keys put web/maintenance true
questions.explanation: All KV interactions go through the `consul kv` subcommand; `consul kv put <key> <value>` writes a single value, and `consul kv get`/`consul kv delete` read and remove keys. `consul write` is not a valid command, `consul config write` manages centralized service-mesh configuration entries (such as proxy-defaults and service-defaults), not arbitrary KV pairs, and `consul keys` is used to manage the gossip encryption keys — not KV entries.

questions.q: An operator bootstraps a new Consul cluster with ACLs enabled and the default policy set to `deny`. A Consul agent starts up and a registered service fails to appear in the catalog. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The agent is using a token that lacks `service:write` permission for the service it is trying to register
ACL replication has not yet completed from the primary datacenter to the local datacenter
The agent must be added to the LAN gossip ring before it is allowed to register any service
The service definition must be placed in a dedicated bootstrap directory before ACLs will accept it
questions.explanation: With a default-deny ACL policy, every write — including service registration done on behalf of the agent — must be authorized by a token that grants the appropriate `service:write` permission for that service name. Operators typically configure each agent with such a token via `acl.tokens.default` or `acl.tokens.agent`. ACL replication is only relevant for multi-datacenter setups, gossip ring membership is unrelated to ACL enforcement, and there is no special bootstrap directory that bypasses ACLs for service definitions.

questions.q: What does Consul Connect provide between services that are part of the service mesh?
choices: A packet-filtering firewall that allows or denies traffic based only on source and destination IP addresses
An external API gateway that terminates public HTTPS for north-south traffic into the cluster
A simple round-robin load balancer that distributes traffic across the upstream service's IP addresses
Mutual TLS authentication and encryption between services using short-lived identity certificates issued by Consul's built-in CA
questions.explanation: Consul Connect adds a service mesh on top of the service catalog. Each service runs behind a sidecar proxy that obtains a short-lived X.509 certificate from Consul's built-in (or configured) CA; the proxies use these certificates for mutual TLS so both endpoints prove their service identity and the traffic is encrypted in transit. IP-based firewalling, north-south API gateway termination and simple round-robin load balancing are not what Connect itself provides — Connect's distinguishing capability is identity-based mTLS plus authorization through intentions.

nodes.title: Service mesh: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A service mesh handles service-to-service communication — discovery, secure connections, traffic control, and observability — outside your application code, usually via a sidecar proxy next to each service. Consul Connect is HashiCorp's implementation.

flashcards.front: What problem does a service mesh solve?
flashcards.back: As services multiply, every app would otherwise re-implement discovery, retries, encryption, and metrics. The mesh moves that into a uniform data plane (sidecar proxies) controlled by a central control plane, so developers get mTLS, routing, and telemetry for free.

flashcards.front: What is the sidecar (data plane) vs the control plane?
flashcards.back: The data plane is the proxy (e.g. Envoy) deployed beside each service instance — it actually carries the traffic. The control plane (Consul servers) distributes configuration, certificates, and intentions to those proxies. Apps talk to localhost; the proxy does the rest.

flashcards.front: How does Consul secure service-to-service traffic?
flashcards.back: Consul Connect issues short-lived TLS certificates to each service identity and the sidecars establish mutual TLS (mTLS) automatically. 'Intentions' are the allow/deny rules that say which service identities may talk to which — authorization by identity, not IP.

A gateway sits at the edge for north-south (client-to-cluster) traffic. A mesh governs east-west (service-to-service) traffic inside the cluster. They complement each other; Consul can do both with mesh gateways for cross-datacentre traffic.

questions.q: Two services, `web` and `db`, are part of the Consul service mesh with intentions enforced and the default intention set to `deny`. A developer needs `web` to be allowed to call `db`. Which action authorizes the call?
choices: Add a host-level firewall rule that permits TCP traffic from the `web` hosts to port 5432 on the `db` hosts
Create an intention with source service `web`, destination service `db`, and action `allow`
Add `db` to the `upstreams` block of `web`'s service definition only
Issue `web` an ACL token granting `kv:read` on the path `db/`
questions.explanation: Intentions are the service-to-service authorization layer of the Consul service mesh. With a default-deny policy, traffic between two mesh services is rejected at the destination's sidecar unless an explicit intention with source = `web`, destination = `db` and action = `allow` exists. A host firewall rule operates one layer below Connect and cannot satisfy intention enforcement; declaring an `upstreams` entry only configures where `web`'s sidecar listens locally and how to discover `db`, not authorization; and ACL tokens with `kv:read` permissions govern KV access, not mesh traffic.

questions.q: How is service-to-service traffic carried inside the mesh when Consul Connect is enabled with a sidecar proxy (the built-in proxy or Envoy)?
choices: The application speaks plain TCP or HTTP to its sidecar on localhost; the sidecar opens an mTLS connection to the destination service's sidecar, which then forwards the request to that service on localhost
Every request from the application makes a synchronous call to the Consul HTTP API to authenticate and locate the peer service
The Consul agent proxies all data-plane traffic itself through its DNS interface on port 8600
Traffic is encrypted hop-by-hop using the gossip-layer symmetric key directly between the two application processes
questions.explanation: In a Connect-enabled mesh, the application stays unaware of TLS: it dials its local sidecar over loopback, the sidecar establishes a mutually authenticated TLS session to the upstream service's sidecar using each side's Connect certificate, and the upstream sidecar then forwards the request to the destination application over loopback. Consul's HTTP API is involved in service discovery and certificate rotation, not in every request; the Consul agent's DNS interface returns A and SRV records but does not proxy data-plane traffic; and the gossip encryption key protects Serf control-plane messages, not application traffic.

questions.q: An operator wants to back up the full state of a Consul cluster — service catalog, KV store, ACLs and sessions — into a single consistent file for disaster recovery. Which command produces that backup?
choices: consul kv export > backup.json
consul members -detailed > backup.json
consul snapshot save backup.snap
consul operator raft list-peers > backup.snap
questions.explanation: `consul snapshot save` asks the current Raft leader to take an atomic point-in-time snapshot of the full FSM — catalog, KV, ACLs, sessions and prepared queries — and writes it to a single file that can later be restored with `consul snapshot restore`. `consul kv export` captures only the KV store under a given prefix; `consul members` lists gossip pool members; and `consul operator raft list-peers` shows the current Raft peer set for troubleshooting consensus, not data.

questions.q: A company runs three Consul datacenters and wants services in each datacenter to be queryable from the others while keeping Raft consensus and LAN gossip local to each datacenter. Which Consul mechanism connects the datacenters?
choices: Configure a bidirectional ACL token sync so that every datacenter's local ACL store mirrors the others
Configure every client agent with the addresses of every datacenter's server agents to join all of them at once
Reconfigure all three datacenters as a single Raft cluster spanning regions so the catalog is globally consistent
Use WAN federation, which joins server agents across datacenters via the WAN gossip pool and lets cross-datacenter queries resolve services in other datacenters
questions.explanation: Consul's WAN federation links datacenters through a separate WAN gossip pool composed only of server agents; each datacenter keeps its own Raft cluster and LAN gossip pool, while cross-datacenter queries (for example, `service.dc2.consul`) are forwarded between server clusters. Mirroring ACL tokens does not transport service catalog data; clients are designed to talk only to local-datacenter servers; and stretching a single Raft cluster across regions is explicitly discouraged because WAN latency destabilizes leader election and replication.
